danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Fra det øjeblik Kutuzov modtog denne nyhed og til felttogets slutning, var al hans aktivitet rettet mod at tilbageholde sine tropper — med myndighed, list og bønner — fra nytteløse angreb, manøvrer eller sammenstød med den døende fjende. Dokhturov drog til Malo-Jaroslavets, men Kutuzov tøvede med hovedhæren og gav ordre til evakuering af Kaluga — et tilbagetog, som han anså for ganske muligt.
Overalt trak Kutuzov sig tilbage, men fjenden flygtede, uden at vente på hans tilbagetog, i den modsatte retning.
Napoleons historieskrivere beskriver hans snedige manøvrer ved Tarutino og Malo-Jaroslavets og gisner om, hvad der ville være sket, hvis Napoleon i tide var trængt ind i de rige sydlige provinser.

Men bortset fra at intet hindrede ham i at rykke ind i de sydlige provinser (for den russiske hær spærrede ikke hans vej), glemmer historieskriverne, at intet kunne have reddet hans hær, for den bar allerede kimen til sin uundgåelige undergang i sig. Hvordan kunne den hær — der havde fundet rigelige forsyninger i Moskva og trådt dem under fode i stedet for at bevare dem, og som ved ankomsten til Smolensk havde plyndret forsyningerne i stedet for at opmagasinere dem — hvordan kunne den hær komme sig i Kaluga-provinsen, der var befolket af russere ligesom dem i Moskva, og hvor ilden havde den samme egenskab at fortære det, der blev sat i brand?
Den hær kunne ikke komme sig noget sted. Siden slaget ved Borodino og plyndringen af Moskva havde den så at sige båret opløsningens kemiske bestanddele i sig.

Medlemmerne af det, der engang havde været en hær — Napoleon selv og alle hans soldater — flygtede uden at vide hvorhen, hver kun optaget af at undslippe så hurtigt som muligt fra denne situation, hvis håbløshed de alle mere eller mindre vagt var bevidste om.

Således skete det, at da der blev holdt krigsråd ved Malo-Jaroslavets, og generalerne foregav at rådslå og fremsatte forskellige meninger, blev alle munde lukket af den mentalitet, den ligetil soldat Mouton udtrykte. Han talte sidst og sagde, hvad de alle følte: at det eneste nødvendige var at komme væk så hurtigt som muligt; og ingen — ikke engang Napoleon — kunne sige noget imod den sandhed, de alle erkendte.

Men selvom de alle indså, at det var nødvendigt at komme væk, følte de stadig skam ved at indrømme, at de måtte flygte. Der var brug for et ydre stød til at overvinde denne skam, og det kom i rette tid. Det var, hvad franskmændene kaldte »le hourra de l'Empereur« — kejserens hurra.

Dagen efter krigsrådet ved Malo-Jaroslavets red Napoleon tidligt om morgenen ud langs sine hærlinjer med sit følge af marskalker og en eskorte, angiveligt for at inspicere hæren og den foregående og den forestående kamplads. Nogle kosakker på strandjagt efter bytte stødte på kejseren og var lige ved at fange ham. Hvis kosakkerne ikke fangede Napoleon dengang, var det, der reddede ham, netop det, der var ved at ødelægge den franske hær: byttet, som kosakkerne kastede sig over. Som ved Tarutino gik de efter plyndring og lod mændene løbe. De ignorerede Napoleon og styrtede efter byttet, og Napoleon slap væk.

Da les enfants du Don — Donens børn — så let kunne have taget kejseren selv midt i hans hær, var det klart, at der ikke var andet for end at flygte så hurtigt som muligt ad den nærmeste, velkendte vej. Napoleon forstod med sin fyrreårige mave det vink, følte ikke sin tidligere smidighed og dristighed, og under indflydelse af den forskrækkelse, kosakkerne havde givet ham, var han straks enig med Mouton og udstedte ordre — som historieskriverne fortæller os — om tilbagetog ad Smolenskvejen.

At Napoleon var enig med Mouton, og at hæren trak sig tilbage, beviser ikke, at Napoleon foranledigede tilbagetoget, men at de kræfter, der påvirkede hele hæren og styrede den ad Mozjajskvejen — det vil sige Smolenskvejen — samtidig virkede på ham.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's energy was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, and clashes with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.
Everywhere Kutuzov retreated, but the enemy, without waiting for his retreat, fled in the opposite direction.

Napoleon's historians describe his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what might have happened if Napoleon had managed to reach the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing south (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and which on arriving at Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could such an army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who lived in Moscow, where fire had the same ability to consume whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself the chemical elements of its own dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from a situation whose hopelessness they all more or less vaguely sensed.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the plain-spoken soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the only thing to do was get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came right on time. The French called it 'the Emperor's hurrah.'

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his marshals and escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. What saved Napoleon wasn't the strength of his forces but the very thing that was destroying the French army: the lure of loot. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When 'the children of the Don' could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, most familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat. Rather, the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.
